paras: The killing of Charles Gross was the whipping to death of a farmer in Pulaski County, Missouri, by a band of masked night riders on the night of June 23, 1888. The cause assigned in the dispatches was that Gross had revealed the secrets of the Agricultural Wheel, a secret organization. Papers across the country ran the story as an outrage by a band likened to the White Caps of Indiana, and one dispatch reported arrests, but no later account of a prosecution was found.

Gross was described as a wealthy farmer and a resident of Pulaski County; no report gives his age, town or race. According to the dispatches, the alleged reason for the attack was that he had divulged the secrets of the Agricultural Wheel.

About midnight on Saturday night, a party of masked riders rode up to Gross's house and dragged him out, or, in the Tribune's version, from his bed. They carried him about a mile away and there whipped him to death. The St. Louis wire of June 25 called the attackers "an organized band similar to the White Caps of Indiana" and added that "Gross was flayed alive," while the New-York Tribune's special said he was "beaten to death."

The Tribune's St. Louis correspondent reported on June 24 that "a number of arrests have been made," but warned that unless a member of the band confessed it would be impossible to punish the killers. No names of those arrested and no report of an inquest, indictment or trial appear in the coverage.

Two St. Louis dispatches carried the story out of Missouri. The first, a Tribune special dated June 24, ran on the New-York Tribune's front page under the headline "Whipped to Death by Oath-Bound Ruffians," and the Camden Evening Telegram printed the same text the same day with the name spelled "Grose." The second, dated June 25 and relaying a telegram from Pulaski County, called the killing "a bold outrage" and was headlined in the Washington Evening Star as the murder of a Missouri farmer "for divulging secrets of the Agricultural Wheel."

Over the next ten days the June 25 wire was reprinted almost word for word in Alexandria, Wilmington, Memphis, Fort Worth, Maysville, Macon, Mississippi, and Hillsboro, Ohio. Headline writers chose "Flayed Alive," "Whipped to Death" and "Whipped to Death by White Caps," and the Fort Worth Daily Gazette's subhead described "A Wealthy Farmer of Missouri Taken from His Bed and Beaten Until Dead." Weekly digests in South Carolina and Minnesota carried shorter versions in early July, the Minnesota paper spelling the name "Gresh"; none of the papers added editorial comment, and no Missouri paper's report was found.

The Washington Critic's condensed brief placed the attack "last night" in its June 25 issue, which would suggest June 24, but the dated Tribune special, the wire's "Saturday night" and the Mower County Transcript's "night of the 23d" all point to June 23. The Critic's version also likened the Agricultural Wheel itself, rather than the band, to the White Caps of Indiana.

reader.title: Killing of Charles Gross
bases: A masked band of night riders, described as an organized band similar to the White Caps of Indiana, took a farmer from his home and whipped him to death for allegedly revealing the secrets of the Agricultural Wheel (A2, A4, A11).

Gross was killed without any lawful authority by a 'party' or 'band' of masked riders whose number is never given, and the papers assign as the cause his alleged betrayal of a secret organization's secrets, a punishment for a supposed offense (A2, A4, A12). The size of the band is not stated, so the group-of-three element rests on the words 'band' and 'party' alone.

Two differently worded St. Louis dispatches, the Tribune's special of June 24 and the June 25 wire relaying a Pulaski County telegram, agree on the victim, county, masked night riders, a beating or whipping to death and the Agricultural Wheel motive (A2, A4); no local Missouri report or follow-up was found.

accounts.label: St. Louis special (New-York Tribune)
accounts.gist: Dated June 24: Gross was dragged from his bed 'last night' by masked night-riders and beaten to death for telling the Wheel's secrets; several arrests had been made but conviction depended on a confession.

accounts.label: St. Louis wire relaying a Pulaski County telegram
accounts.gist: Dated June 25: on Saturday night about midnight an organized band like the White Caps of Indiana took Gross from his house, carried him a mile and whipped him to death; most versions add that he was 'flayed alive'.

accounts.label: Condensed news-summary version
accounts.gist: Masked men took Gross from his house 'last night', carried him a mile away and whipped him to death; here the Wheel itself, not the band, is likened to the White Caps.

framing.detail: The New-York Tribune headlined the special 'Whipped to Death by Oath-Bound Ruffians' and called the killers 'the murderers'.
Most papers ran the June 25 wire nearly verbatim, calling it 'a bold outrage' and heading it 'Flayed Alive', 'Whipped to Death' or 'Whipped to Death by White Caps', with no editorial comment.
